study_identification.title: Regional, circuit and network heterogeneity of brain abnormalities in psychiatric disorders

study_characteristics.study_objective: To characterize the heterogeneity of gray matter volume (GMV) differences across multiple psychiatric disorders at regional, circuit, and network levels using normative modeling, and to test whether anatomically heterogeneous regional GMV deviations are functionally coupled to common areas and networks.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) with site and sex modeled as random effects (random slopes, intercepts, and noise). Partial-pooling approach with shared prior distributions over site-specific and sex-specific model parameters. Site effects were validated using linear support vector machines (LSVMs) with balanced accuracy at chance level (50%), confirming that resulting deviations were not contaminated by residual site effects (Supplementary Table 2). Data cells with <10 HCs for a particular sex at a given site were excluded. Sites with <10 cases total were excluded (N=217 scans).
site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper provides comprehensive details on how site effects were handled through HBR methodology, including the specific modeling approach (random effects with partial pooling) and validation that site effects were successfully removed.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: When using multisite data, scanner- and site-related variability introduce artefactual variance that confounds the results of any subsequent analyses. These confounding effects present as site-correlated biases that cannot be explained by biological heterogeneity between samples. To account for these site-related effects, we built our normative model using HBR, which successfully accommodates signal and noise variance in multisite data by estimating different but connected mean and variance components through shared prior distributions across sites. ... The HBRs modelled site and sex effects with random slopes, intercepts and noise, to model GMV as a function of age, sex and site in the training data, yielding estimates of normative regional GMV variance and predictive uncertainty. Importantly, based on a partial-pooling approach, shared prior distributions were imposed over site-specific and sex-specific model parameters. These shared priors assume that, while the model parameters for each site and sex are different, they are drawn from a common distribution. These shared priors thus regularize the model parameters and prevent the model from overfitting small batches for a given sex or site. ... We also evaluated the model's efficacy in partitioning site-related variance in the data using linear support vector machines (LSVMs)... Here, a balanced accuracy at chance level (50%) indicated that the resulting deviations were not contaminated by residual site effects, as confirmed in Supplementary Table 2. ... For the model to accurately parse variance attributable to age, sex and site, sufficient observations are required for any given combination of these variables. We therefore excluded data cells containing less than ten HCs for a particular sex at a given site. If this exclusion procedure resulted in less than ten cases in total from any given site, the entire site was excluded, resulting in the exclusion of 217 scans.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To assess model generalizability, we used five-fold cross-validation applied to the HC_train cohort (n = 1,196 HC individuals, 55% male). Specifically, we partitioned the HC_train cohort into five folds. Within each fold, we trained HBR models on 80% of participants, using age, sex and site as covariates, withholding 20% of the participants for estimating generalization performance. This procedure was repeated five times so that regional GMV values for all participants in the HC_train group were predicted once. As above, we estimated deviation z maps for every individual and identified extreme deviations. This procedure is standard in machine learning and provides approximately unbiased estimates of the true generalization ability. For each fold in the cross-validation, we assessed model fit for each brain region by evaluating three performance metrics: (1) explained variance, (2) the mean standardized log-loss and (3) the standardized mean-squared error as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Multiple analytical approaches were used: (1) Group-based permutation tests (10,000 permutations with generalized Pareto tail approximation) to compare case vs. control overlap at regional, circuit, and network levels, with FDR correction (p_FDR < 0.05, two-tailed); (2) Spatial permutation tests using Hungarian spin tests (cortex) and random shuffling (subcortex) to evaluate whether observed differences were driven by total deviation burden or preferential circuit/network involvement; (3) Mann-Whitney U-tests to compare extreme deviation burden between cases and controls; (4) Linear support vector machines (LSVMs) to validate site effect removal; (5) Pearson correlations between scan quality (IQR) and deviation burden; (6) Threshold-weighted analyses integrating results across multiple thresholds; (7) Comparison of overlap differences between regional and circuit levels to evaluate multi-scale heterogeneity.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Individual GMV deviations showed extreme regional heterogeneity (<7% overlap in any region), but were embedded within common functional circuits and networks (up to 56% overlap), with the salience-ventral attention network implicated transdiagnostically.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: At the regional level, extreme GMV deviations rarely occurred in the same location across individuals with the same diagnosis (maximum overlap <7% across 1,032 regions in any disorder). However, at the circuit level (regions functionally coupled to deviant areas), overlap was substantially higher, reaching 33% in controls and 39-53% in clinical groups. Using group-based permutation testing, SCZ and MDD showed significantly greater circuit-level overlap across wide swathes of cortex (~75% and ~31% of areas respectively, p_FDR < 0.05), with similar patterns at uncorrected levels in ASD, OCD, and BP. At the network level, SCZ showed greater overlap in all networks except thalamus and basal ganglia, while MDD showed greater overlap in all cortical networks. The salience/ventral attention network was implicated across five of six disorders. Using spatial permutation tests (controlling for deviation burden), only three areas in BP and one in MDD showed preferential circuit-level involvement at FDR-corrected levels, while network-level analysis revealed preferential involvement of salience/ventral attention in SCZ and dorsal attention/medial temporal networks in ADHD. For positive GMV deviations, findings were less pronounced, with ASD showing greater circuit- and network-level overlap under group-based testing. Overall, 76-89% of cases showed at least one negative extreme deviation (vs. 76% in controls), with BP, MDD, OCD, and SCZ showing significantly higher negative deviation burden (p < 0.003). Model validation showed adequate fit (explained variance, MSLL, SMSE in Supplementary Fig. 3) and successful site effect removal (balanced accuracy ~50% in Supplementary Table 2).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Considerable overlap between cases and controls, with ~50% of clinical participants showing relatively low deviation burden (<3 deviations), suggesting brain changes in psychiatric illness may be subtle and complex. Limited sensitivity of GMV measures to map pathophysiologically relevant changes; other modalities (functional, molecular imaging) may reveal stronger case-control separation. Multi-site data pooling required due to small single-site samples, resulting in different acquisition, recruitment, and clinical assessment protocols across sites. Site-related variance was parsed using HBR, but future work could extend to larger normative samples. No assessment of correlations with symptom profiles, age of onset, illness duration, medication exposure, or disease severity across disorders. Methods suited for characterizing overlap but not individual differences in behavior. Lack of harmonized transdiagnostic clinical protocols with extensive symptom sampling. Age-specific effects not examined (case-control differences may vary across lifespan). Use of DSM/ICD diagnostic categories rather than syndrome-focused approaches. Choice of parcellation affects observable overlap levels; group-based (not individualized) parcellation was used. FC patterns may be altered in diagnosed individuals, affecting coupling between deviant and other areas. Study focused primarily on control data from same scanners as clinical data to avoid site-diagnosis confounds.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The findings suggest that phenotypic differences between cases with the same diagnosis may arise from heterogeneous localization of regional deviations, while phenotypic similarities may be attributable to dysfunction of common functional circuits and networks. Treatment targets identified through spatial permutation analysis may only be relevant for subsets of patients (10-50% overlap), indicating that current approaches attempting to identify a single common therapeutic target for each diagnosis will have limited success. More comprehensive understanding of patient-specific brain changes and their network context necessary for effective, personally tailored interventions. The common involvement of prefrontal and parietal circuits, and salience/ventral attention network across disorders may be a marker of transdiagnostic psychological distress. Results challenge classical views that distinct diagnoses are associated with dysfunction in specific circuits, suggesting each disorder is associated with complex changes affecting diverse neural systems. Many circuit/network-level effects appear driven by deviation burden rather than preferential targeting, suggesting an underlying random process as a candidate generative mechanism rather than targeted pathophysiological process. Future work should: (1) characterize relationship between GMV deviations and interindividual symptom expression differences; (2) investigate genetic and environmental contributions to individual-specific deviations; (3) develop harmonized transdiagnostic multisite clinical protocols; (4) consider age-specific effects; (5) focus on syndromes rather than traditional diagnoses; (6) use individualized parcellations; (7) investigate altered FC patterns in diagnosed individuals.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a landmark multi-scale study demonstrating that regional heterogeneity of GMV deviations is a general feature of psychiatric illness, but these deviations aggregate within common functional circuits and networks. The study adapted lesion network mapping techniques for use with normative modeling, introducing two complementary null models (group-based and spatial permutation tests) to distinguish natural case-control differences from preferential circuit/network involvement. Notably, the study included resting-state fMRI data from an independent HCP sample (n=150, lowest motion subjects from S900 release) to map functional circuitry of deviant regions under normative conditions. The HCP fMRI preprocessing included minimal preprocessing pipeline, ICA-FIX artifact removal, and global signal regression (GSR) despite its controversies, justified by enhanced anatomical specificity and behavioral prediction. Circuit-level analysis used seed-based FC with TFCE thresholding (p_FWE < 0.025) and two parcel-mapping thresholds (50% and 75%) to ensure robustness. Box-Cox transformation was applied to regional GMV estimates to ensure normality before modeling. The study examined both 10-network (7 cortical + 3 subcortical) and 20-network (17 cortical + 3 subcortical) parcellations, with consistent findings. Full dataset details are provided in Supplementary Table 1, including references for each contributing dataset (ABIDE I/II, ASRB, FEMS, MON, IMpACT-NL, KANMDD, MITASD, OCDPG, RUSMDD, SPAINOCD, TOP15, WASHASD, YoDA). Code and data availability: PCNtoolkit v0.16 used for normative modeling; analysis code available at https://github.com/ashlea-segal/crossdisorder_multiscale_gmv_heterogeneity.git; cortical surface renderings generated using plotSurfaceROIBoundary. The study represents one of the largest aggregations of case-control psychiatric neuroimaging data outside the ENIGMA consortium.
